desc: Colloquially used for the whole thing. Legally, the card is the Führerschein and the right to drive is the Fahrerlaubnis.
What you actually apply for. Klasse B = cars up to 3.5 t.
You must train through one — there is no self-taught route in Germany.
Sits next to you with their own pedals. Your best ally for exam tactics.
In Berlin it's part of LABO. Processes your application before you may take any exam.

en: Berlin state office for citizen & regulatory affairs
desc: Landesamt für Bürger- und Ordnungsangelegenheiten — the authority behind Berlin's licence office.
Where Anmeldung happens. Not the same as the licence office.
Proof you live in Berlin. Prerequisite for basically everything.
The paper you got at Anmeldung. Sometimes requested with your application.
Quick vision screening at an optician; the certificate is needed for your application.
One-day course (9 units of 45 min). Certificate never expires for licence purposes.
35×45 mm, neutral face. Same standard as passport photos.
The authority's green light that lets DEKRA/TÜV examine you. Your Fahrschule receives it.
30 questions on a touchscreen; bookable in English. Max 10 error points.
≈55 minutes with an examiner in the back seat. Conducted in German.
The 12 basic theory topics every licence class shares.
Extra topics for class B: vehicle tech, trailers, loading.
12 legally required lessons: 5 country road, 4 Autobahn, 3 night.
One of the Sonderfahrten — higher speeds outside towns.
Sonderfahrt in the dark — lights, glare, wildlife.
Parking, turning, emergency braking — tested in the practical exam.
Exam warm-up: show tyre tread, lights, fluids on request.
What the Fahrschule charges to take you to each exam — on top of DEKRA/TÜV fees.
The driving school's sign-up fee covering theory lessons and admin.
45 minutes. No legal minimum number — your instructor decides when you're ready.
Your first 2 years. Serious violations mean an expensive seminar (Aufbauseminar) and extended probation.
What you must attend (and pay for) after an A-violation during Probezeit.
National register of traffic violations. 8 points = licence gone.
Feared evaluation after drink-driving or 8 points. Avoid at all costs.
The single most important exam topic. 5-point questions live here.
The upside-down triangle sign (206 is STOP, 205 is yield).
Default priority rule at unmarked junctions — the car from your right goes first.
Yellow diamond sign. You have priority until it's cancelled.
Blue arrow sign. In Berlin, many allow cyclists AGAINST the direction — watch out.
Pedestrians have absolute priority. Failing to yield = failed exam.
Blue sign with pedestrians/house. Walking pace only, pedestrians may use the whole street.
In a jam on the Autobahn: leftmost lane moves left, everyone else right. Forming it is mandatory.
Berlin's inner city (inside the S-Bahn ring). Green sticker (grüne Plakette) required.
Off-limits for cars — also a favourite exam trap when turning right.
Cyclists set the pace and may ride side by side; cars are guests (if allowed at all).
The X sign before every level crossing: the train ALWAYS has priority.
Train mostly on automatic, do a short manual validation — licence stays unrestricted.
If you do the exam on automatic without B197, your licence is restricted to automatics.
Drive from 17 with a registered adult companion until you turn 18.
As in: 'Haben Sie einen Erste-Hilfe-Nachweis?' — do you have the certificate?
The word you want to hear. Its evil twin: 'nicht bestanden'.
What people call the Fahrerlaubnisbehörde in everyday speech.
Swapping a foreign licence for a German one. For EU licences: optional, no exams. For non-EU licences like Argentine ones: this is your main route.
The 185-days-per-year rule deciding which country may issue your licence. Living in Berlin means Germany is the only country that may licence you.
How German law labels countries like Argentina. Different, stricter conversion rules than EU licences.
The official list of non-EU countries and how much of the German exam their licence holders are spared. Which line your country is on decides everything.
The phrase to use at the counter when you show your Argentine licence.
How long your foreign licence still counts in Germany after you move in. Miss it and driving becomes a criminal offence.
§ 21 StVG — a criminal offence, not a mere fine. What driving on an expired-recognition foreign licence becomes.
Your Argentine licence generally needs an officially accepted German translation (ADAC or a sworn translator).
Done by a court-sworn translator (vereidigter Übersetzer) and stamped — the version authorities accept.
Mapping your Argentine categories onto German classes so the authority knows what to issue.
A translator authorised by a German court; their stamp makes a translation official.
The scarcest resource in Berlin. Book online early; check daily for cancellations.
Berlin publishes which application dates are currently being processed — use it to estimate your wait.
What the authority grants once your application is approved; the exams can't be taken before it.
Temporary paper you get right after passing the practical exam, so you can drive before the card arrives.
Not a real word you'll hear — but memorise the exam formulas: reaction, braking, stopping distance!
The car's mandatory technical check — 'der TÜV' colloquially.
